title: Public-institution quality converts policy mandates into procurement prices, firm access, regulatory predictability, and private-sector outcomes
source_unit: World Bank, Institutions and Prosperity: Public Institutions for Enabling the Private Sector
geography: Public procurement and regulatory institutions, firms, markets, and government contracting across comparative country evidence and named country cases

denominator.unit: public institution implementation and governance framework

organizational_dimensions.value: personnel, financial resources, information systems, and management practices
organizational_dimensions.unit: four dimensions in the World Bank Public Institutions Assessment Framework

governance_dimensions.unit: three cross-cutting governance dimensions in the framework

conversion_chain.value: mandate, resources, systems, management, governance, implementation, and development outcomes

within_government_variation.value: institutional capacity and policy implementation can vary substantially among bodies in the same government

observations.method: World Bank synthesis of institutional evidence and a framework for diagnosing organizational and governance constraints in individual public bodies.
observations.uncertainty: The framework identifies bottlenecks and pathways but does not imply that one reform dimension produces the same private-sector or public outcome in every institution.
observations.subgroup: Ministries, regulators, procurement agencies, local governments, firms, suppliers, workers, consumers, oversight bodies, and affected communities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional reform can be slow or costly and may create new compliance burdens; weak performance in one agency does not establish failure of an entire state or market.

observations.period: 2026; procurement personnel quality and contracting performance

denominator.unit: country-level procurement personnel and government-contracting comparison frame

personnel_quality_outcome.unit: quality of procurement personnel and ease of contracting with government

contracting_components.value: steps required, time required, and sophistication of e-procurement platforms

gdp_control.value: association remains significant at the 90 percent confidence level after controlling for GDP per capita

procurement_effects.value: fewer cost overruns, delays, renegotiations, and stronger firm access when personnel, systems, payments, and management are capable

observations.method: World Bank use of OECD MAPS procurement assessments and country-level contracting indicators, with a reported association rather than a universal causal estimate.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is country-level and observational; it does not identify firm-specific contract awards, causal personnel changes, final prices, delivery quality, or downstream consumer incidence.
observations.subgroup: Public procurement officers, contracting firms, small suppliers, public buyers, e-procurement providers, workers, taxpayers, and service users.
observations.counterinterpretation: Procurement personnel quality may partly proxy broader administrative capacity, market structure, or fiscal conditions rather than independently causing contracting ease.

lowest_highest_performer_price_gap.unit: percent higher prices paid by the lowest-performing procurement units than the highest-performing units for similar products, approximately

procurement_levers.value: competent staff, competitive compensation, timely payments, strong information systems, and stable management

public_value_risk.value: price dispersion, delays, renegotiations, and cost overruns

capture_controls.value: accountability, independence, transparency, oversight, and more public procurement information

observations.method: World Bank named-country case synthesis using procurement performance evidence and comparative institutional analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The 55 percent difference is a case-level comparison and not a national average or proof that personnel quality alone caused the price gap; product, buyer, contract, and market differences may remain.
observations.subgroup: Italian purchasing units, procurement officers, suppliers, public budgets, competing firms, taxpayers, and users of procured goods and services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher prices may sometimes reflect quality, urgency, contract terms, or legitimate specification differences rather than waste or corruption.

observations.period: 2026; regulatory capacity, tenure, and market predictability

regulatory_constraints.value: limited personnel expertise, outdated information systems, management weakness, and political or commercial influence

regulatory_effects.value: competition, standards enforcement, service quality, compliance, and market confidence

peru_leadership_effect.value: frequent leadership changes delayed key regulatory milestones

transparency_effect.value: greater transparency and accountability helped reduce regulatory uncertainty

observations.method: World Bank case reconstruction of Peru telecommunications milestones, leadership tenure, legal and regulatory acts, and institutional-governance conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The case demonstrates a governance mechanism and timing relationship, not a general causal estimate of leadership tenure on prices, investment, service quality, or consumer welfare.
observations.subgroup: Telecommunications regulators, ministries, operators, infrastructure firms, investors, workers, consumers, and public oversight bodies.
observations.counterinterpretation: Leadership turnover can sometimes correct capture or accelerate reform; transparency may correlate with broader political or sectoral changes rather than independently reducing uncertainty.

related_sources.claim: World Bank report PDF and detailed evidence underlying the public-institutions framework.
World Bank reproducibility resources linked from the report page.

boundary: This record adds a public-institution-to-firm-market route linking personnel, resources, information systems, management, independence, accountability, transparency, procurement prices, contracting ease, regulatory milestones, competition, and service quality. It is not firm respondent data, consumer-level price incidence, a universal causal estimate, proof of corruption, or evidence that institutional reform automatically creates private-sector growth or public trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official World Bank report page and linked overview were reviewed; institutional dimensions, procurement personnel/contracting association, Italy price dispersion, regulatory capacity, and Peru telecommunications case claims were cross-checked.
